content.title: Developing nursing and midwifery essential for improved healthcare in East Africa
content.author: Iqra Paintern
content.description: Governments in the East Africa Community countries need to continue investing in the education of nurses and midwives as these professionals are the cornerstone of improving access to quality health care in the region said the Chief Guest, first lady of Uganda and Minister for Karamoja Affairs, Janet Museveni at the School of Nursing and Midwifery's Regional Alumni Conference in Kampala. "We in East Africa need to continue to develop nurses and midwifery professionals by providing them with tools to perform their work in the changing world.... We need to provide them with opportunities for professional development and a working environment suitable to their needs so that they can better serve the patients," she said. The two-day conference, with the theme of "Nurses and Midwives Leading the Way: Making an Impact", was attended by government officials, healthcare providers, nursing and midwifery professionals and AKU alumni from across Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. Dr Amalberga Kassangala, Chief Nursing Officer, Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Tanzania, highlighted that nurses and midwives with a bachelor's or graduate degree can advance to becoming managers and leaders, provide improved nursing care and better meet the needs of an rapidly evolving healthcare system. She also outlined the importance of the role played by stakeholders in meeting the healthcare challenges faced by the EAC countries. Nurses are the cornerstone of a health workforce and that the partnership between AKU and Johnson & Johnson has ensured that talented nurses from all backgrounds have the opportunity to enhance their knowledge while continuing their clinical practice said Frank Welvaert, CSR Director, Europe Middle East and Africa, Johnson & Johnson. He also stressed that AKU graduates were equipped to respond to local and regional health needs and were empowered to make a difference. Education has to meet the needs of complex changes in healthcare. Dr Robert Armstrong, Dean of AKU's Medical College in East Africa noted the importance of collaboration between medicine and nursing. The University is working towards developing a Faculty of Health Sciences curriculum that will include areas of synergy aimed at producing effective leaders interested in resolving the most pressing issues. SONAM has over 2,000 alumni in nursing and midwifery within East Africa, many of whom serve as clinicians, educators and leaders at several levels of healthcare in the community and in hospitals.   A special session was held in honour of Professor Yasmin Amarsi, Founding Dean of SONAM in East Africa for her distinguished 35-year career at the University. During her career she led significant initiatives to bolster nursing and midwifery in the region. Most recently, her efforts are to harmonise nursing education and practice in East Africa, allowing nurses and midwives to engage in careers in the region.
